newsitem.title: USA: Fla. judge reserves ruling on tobacco case motion.
newsitem.headline: Fla. judge reserves ruling on tobacco case motion.

text.p: A Florida judge on Tuesday heard arguments but did not rule on a motion to dismiss a charge of conspiracy to commit fraud in a wrongful death lawsuit against R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co.

After hearing arguments, Duval County Circuit Judge Bernard Nachman indicated he would likely grant a partial summary judgment on the Reynolds motion to remove the conspiracy count from a lawsuit filed by the sister of a smoker who died of lung cancer.
R.J. Reynolds is a unit of RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp.
The lawsuit was initially filed as a product liability case for Jean Connor, a longtime smoker who died of lung cancer in 1995 at age 49.

After Connor died, her lawyer, Norwood Wilner, refiled the suit as a wrongful death case with Connor's sister, Dana Raulerson, as the plaintiff on behalf of Connor's estate and her three children. Trial is set for April 7.
The lawsuit contends tobacco companies perpetrated fraud by hiding the dangers of cigarette smoking or by presenting smoking as healthful and fun when their own research showed it to be dangerous.

Paul Crist, an attorney for R.J. Reynolds, told Nachman there was no evidence that Jean Connor had seen, heard or relied on information contained in cigarette advertising in making her decision to smoke.
"The plaintiff is really seeking to assert that there was fraud in the air and the fraud somehow touched Jean Connor," Crist said.

Raulerson's attorney, Wilner, countered that Connor relied on advertising for Salem cigarettes, the brand she smoked, which said that Salems were "springtime fresh." He compared the cigarettes to rat poison, asking if rat poison would be advertised as "springtime fresh?"
Wilner also argued that Connor indirectly relied on advertising because she was influenced by the opinions of family and friends who were in turn influenced by tobacco company publicity.
Nachman said he was "not too thrilled" with that line of argument. He indicated he would likely grant a partial summary judgment.
"I have grave doubts that could be proven (or) that's good law," he said.
The judge ordered the two sides to submit proposed written orders by Friday but did not say when he would rule.
